questions.prompt: What is the behavior of calling `try_set`?
options: Well-defined: the failure order is silently strengthened to `acquire`
Ill-formed: the compiler must reject the failure order
Undefined behavior: the failure order may not be `release` or `acq_rel`
Well-defined: a failed CAS performs a release store of the old value
questions.explanation: A failed compare-exchange is just a load, so a release failure order makes no sense, and the standard makes `failure` being `release` or `acq_rel` a precondition violation, which is undefined behavior. It is not ill-formed: the orders are ordinary function arguments, and GCC only warns with `-Winvalid-memory-model`. Some implementations happen to strengthen the order, but nothing guarantees it.

questions.prompt: Which of these types does the standard guarantee to be lock-free on every implementation?
options: `std::atomic<bool>`
`std::atomic_flag`
`std::atomic<int>`
`std::atomic<void*>`
questions.explanation: `std::atomic_flag` is the only one of these guaranteed lock-free; it is the primitive from which an implementation can build locks for everything else. `std::atomic<int>`, `std::atomic<bool>` and `std::atomic<void*>` are lock-free on every mainstream platform, but the standard leaves it to the implementation, which is why `is_always_lock_free` and the `ATOMIC_..._LOCK_FREE` macros exist. C++20's `atomic_signed_lock_free` aliases are the other guaranteed option.

questions.prompt: Nodes are recycled through a free list instead of deleted, and `next` is atomic so that reusing a node is not a data race. Thread T1 runs `pop` on the stack `A -> B -> C`, reads `old = A` and `old->next == B`, and is preempted before its CAS. Thread T2 pops A, pops B, then pushes the recycled A, so the stack is `A -> C`. What happens when T1 resumes and its CAS runs?
options: The CAS fails because the stack changed, and T1 retries
The CAS succeeds and makes the removed node B the head, losing C
The CAS succeeds and correctly leaves `C` as the head
The CAS blocks until T2's operations are complete
questions.explanation: A compare-and-swap compares only the bits of the head pointer, and the head holds A again, so T1's CAS succeeds and installs its stale `next`, B, as the new head. B was popped and C is no longer reachable. This is the ABA problem: the value went from A to something else and back to A, and the CAS cannot tell. A version tag or a reclamation scheme that prevents reuse is needed to fix it.

questions.prompt: Two threads run at the same time, one calling `left()` and the other `right()`, with no synchronization. What does the standard say?
options: It is a data race, so the behavior is undefined
It is not a data race, but each counter may lose increments to the other thread
It is not a data race; sharing a cache line can only affect performance
It is implementation-defined, depending on the cache line size
questions.explanation: `a` and `b` are separate memory locations, so the two threads never access the same location and there is no data race. Each thread's counter ends at exactly one million. Sharing a cache line causes false sharing, which can make both loops much slower, but the memory model is defined in terms of memory locations, not cache lines. Adjacent bit-fields would be different, because they share one memory location.

questions.prompt: In C++17 and later, is this call well-defined?
options: Yes: since C++17 the failure order may be stronger than the success order
No: the failure order may never be stronger than the success order
No: `relaxed` is not allowed as a success order for compare-exchange
It is well-defined only for `compare_exchange_weak`
questions.explanation: Before C++17, the failure order could not be stronger than the success order. P0418, adopted for C++17, removed that rule, so the only remaining restriction is that failure is not `release` or `acq_rel`. GCC 16 still emits a `-Winvalid-memory-model` warning that reflects the old rule, which makes the second option tempting, but the call is valid.

questions.prompt: Assuming `std::atomic<Node*>` is lock-free and only `push` and `pop` operations that each succeed with one CAS touch `head`, which progress guarantee does this `push` provide?
options: Wait-free: every call finishes in a bounded number of steps
Blocking: a preempted thread can stop all others
Lock-free but not wait-free: some thread always finishes, but one thread can keep losing
Not even obstruction-free
questions.explanation: A strong CAS fails only because another thread changed `head`, which means another push or pop succeeded, so the system as a whole always makes progress. Nothing bounds how often one particular thread loses, so a thread can starve, which rules out wait-free. No thread ever waits for another to release anything, so it is not blocking. Whether the hardware CAS itself always lets someone win is the implementation's lock-free promise, which the standard only encourages.

questions.prompt: What does [intro.progress] *require* of executions of lock-free atomic operations?
options: Every lock-free execution completes in a bounded number of steps
If only one thread is not blocked in a standard library function, its lock-free execution completes; that one of several concurrent executions completes is only encouraged
At least one of several concurrent lock-free executions must complete
Nothing: lock-freedom is a non-normative note
questions.explanation: The normative requirement is the obstruction-free property: a lock-free execution in the only thread that is not blocked shall complete. The stronger property that at least one of several concurrent lock-free executions completes is stated with *should*, because load-linked and store-conditional hardware can let threads repeatedly invalidate each other. The first option is wait-freedom, which the standard never promises.

questions.prompt: `ok` is `false` after this call. What does the standard guarantee about `e`?
options: `e` is unchanged, because a failed CAS writes nothing
`e` holds the value read from `a`, which may still be 5 if the failure was spurious
`e` holds a value different from 5
`e` is indeterminate
questions.explanation: On failure, compare-exchange atomically loads the current value into `expected`. `compare_exchange_weak` may also fail spuriously even when the values were equal, so `e` can still be 5. Only `compare_exchange_strong` guarantees that a failure means the values really differed, which is what the third option assumes. That is why `weak` belongs inside a retry loop.
